opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly my answer has shifted quite a bit over the years.

When I was a PhD student, and even in my early years as a researcher at NVIDIA, contribution meant something very concrete and personal. It meant: did I come up with the idea? Did I write the code? Is my name first on the paper? I measured myself by the papers I wrote and the techniques I personally invented. With work like the early GAN-based image translation projects, I was deep in the details, tuning the loss functions, staring at generated images at two in the morning. That felt like research.

As I took on more of a leadership role, that definition stopped fitting. At first it was uncomfortable. You spend your days in meetings, reviewing other people's experiments, thinking about compute allocation and hiring, and at the end of the day you ask yourself, "What did I actually do today?" There's a sense of loss, because the joy of directly solving a problem with your own hands is very real.

Over time I've come to see contribution at a different level. One part is choosing the right problems. In AI the field moves so fast that picking the right direction often matters more than executing well on a mediocre one. When we decided to push seriously on world foundation models and physical AI, the Cosmos effort, that was a bet. Nobody can write that by themselves. The contribution is in seeing that robotics and autonomous systems need a model that understands how the physical world evolves, and then convincing people and organizing resources so it can actually happen.

The second part is building the team and the environment. If I can find talented people, give them a problem worth their energy, protect them from distractions, and help them grow, the total output is far larger than anything I could produce alone. Seeing a junior researcher go from uncertain to leading a major piece of the system is now one of the most satisfying parts of my job.

The third part, which I think is underrated, is that modern AI research is increasingly a systems effort. Data curation, tokenizers, training infrastructure, evaluation, safety guardrails, each is a real research contribution, but none of it matters unless it comes together. Part of my role is making sure those pieces fit, and that the people doing the less glamorous work, like building data pipelines, get recognized, because without them there is no model.

So if you'd asked me ten years ago, I would have said contribution means inventing a clever algorithm. Today I'd say it means helping the field move forward, sometimes through ideas, but more often through direction, people, and building things at a scale that open new possibilities for others. Releasing models openly so researchers and developers around the world can build on them is also contribution. It's less about my name and more about impact.

That said, I still try to stay close to the technical details. I read papers, look at results, and argue about architectures with the team. I think a research leader who loses touch with the technology starts making bad decisions. So it's a balance: zoomed out enough to see the direction, close enough to know what's actually real.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts personal research output with broader leadership contributions, but does not connect pressure for state-of-the-art results to researchers feeling they must outperform one another.

r002.rationale: It presents finding talented people, helping them grow, and seeing a junior researcher lead a major effort as satisfying ways to contribute.

r003.rationale: It says openly released models let researchers and developers build on them, but does not describe partners solving problems more efficiently as validation of the team’s contribution.

r004.rationale: The response broadens contribution beyond personally inventing an algorithm, but does not state that contributing to AI does not require outperforming others.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because the shift was not gradual for me. It felt like a different job with the same title on the business card.

When I was a researcher, contribution was very concrete. You have an idea, you run the experiments, you write the paper, and at the end you can point to it and say, this is mine. I came out of that culture. My PhD at Maryland, then MERL, then early days at Nvidia Research working on GANs and image synthesis. The satisfaction was very direct. You touch the thing.

Now I lead a fairly large team, and for a long time I had this quiet anxiety that I was not contributing anymore. I was in meetings. I was deciding priorities. I was arguing for compute. Nobody writes "attended planning meeting" in the acknowledgments section of a paper.

But my view has changed, and I think it changed in three ways.

The first is about scale. In the GAN era, a strong individual or a group of three people could move the field. Today, with foundation models, with video world models, the unit of research is a team of forty, sixty, a hundred people, with data pipelines, infrastructure, evaluation, safety, all of it. No individual sees the whole thing anymore. So the question becomes: who makes sure the whole thing is coherent? Who decides that we should bet on video generation as a path to physical AI, two or three years before it is obvious? That is a research contribution. It just doesn't look like one from the inside.

The second is about taste. When you're an individual contributor, your taste shows up in your own work. As a manager, your taste shows up in what you say no to. I say no far more often than I say yes now. And every no is a bet. I think a lot of the real intellectual work of a research leader is in those judgments, which problems are ripe, which are fashionable but shallow, which young researcher should be protected from the roadmap for a year because they are onto something.

The third one is more personal. I used to measure myself by what I could do. Now I measure myself by what the team can do that it could not do before. If someone on my team gives a talk and the audience is impressed, and I had almost nothing visible to do with it, that is now the best day for me. It took me a few years to feel that honestly rather than just say it.

I'll add one caveat, because I don't want to make it sound too clean. I still miss writing code. I still read papers every morning before meetings start, partly because if I lose touch with the details, my judgments get worse, and judgment is the only thing I bring now. So I don't think the manager fully replaces the researcher. The researcher just moves one level up, and has to accept being less visible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research scale and managerial judgment, but does not connect pressure to achieve state-of-the-art results with researchers’ need to outperform one another.

r002.rationale: It mentions protecting a young researcher and measuring success by the team’s growth, but does not clearly present cultivating a new generation of research talent as a way to contribute to AI research.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss partners or their problem-solving efficiency after using a model.

r004.rationale: It describes team-level contribution, but does not state that contributing to AI does not require outperforming others.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that I’ve broadened my view of what a contribution looks like. As a researcher, you tend to focus on the problem you’re solving: Is the idea novel? Does it work? Can you explain it clearly in a paper? Those things still matter to me, but as a manager, I also have to ask whether I’m helping other people do their best work.

Sometimes that means discussing a technical idea. Sometimes it means helping someone choose a direction, connecting people with complementary expertise, or removing an obstacle. You may not be the person who comes up with the key insight, but you can help create the conditions for that insight to happen.

There’s also a balance to learn. Research needs room for uncertainty, so you want to provide enough direction to make progress while giving people ownership of the problem. For me, contributing becomes less about how much I can personally do and more about how much I can help the team discover together.

sol-6.1.text:
As a researcher, I used to think of contribution mainly in terms of the work I did directly—the idea, the experiments, the paper. As a manager, I’ve come to think more about how I can help other people do great research.

That includes finding the right problems, bringing together people with complementary strengths, and making sure they have the resources and freedom to explore. Sometimes my most useful contribution is asking a question or helping remove an obstacle, rather than proposing the solution myself.

You also have to become comfortable with the fact that the people on your team may understand a particular problem much better than you do. Your job is to support their judgment while helping connect their work to a broader direction. So I still care deeply about the technical work, but I see enabling other researchers as an important contribution in its own right.
